notes.meaning: "Again" looks back to the three-year famine in chapter 21. God was angry because Israel had sinned, likely by joining the revolts of Absalom and Sheba against David. God does not tempt anyone to sin. The parallel story in 1 Chronicles 21:1 says Satan stirred David up, and God allowed it as a just judge.

David told Joab to count the fighting men across the whole land. "From Dan to Beersheba" means from the far north to the far south. Counting the people was not wrong in itself, since Moses did it at God's command. David's sin was his pride. He wanted to know his strength so he could trust in it instead of in God.

Joab was not a very godly man, yet he saw that this plan was foolish. He spoke kindly: may God make the people a hundred times more, and may you live to see it. But why do you want to do this? Some things that are not sinful become sin when our hearts take wrong pride in them. It is good to have a friend who warns us when we act in pride.
Joab and the army leaders objected, but the king would not listen. So they went out to do the count. It is a sad thing when powerful people have helpers who will serve them even in something wrong.

These verses trace the counters' journey. They started east of the Jordan River and then went north to Dan, near Sidon. Next they went to the old city of Tyre on the mainland and the towns where Canaanites still lived. Last they went south to Beersheba. "Tahtim-hodshi" is a puzzle, but it may mean land Israel had recently taken. Soldiers may have gone along to help with the hard work or to keep order.
The count took almost ten months and caused a lot of trouble across the country. Even then it was not fully finished. First Chronicles says the tribes of Levi and Benjamin were not counted.

Joab gave the totals: 800,000 fighting men in Israel and 500,000 in Judah. First Chronicles 21:5 gives different numbers. Older commentators explain this in different ways. Some say one book included the king's standing army and the other did not. Some think the numbers were rounded. Others think a copyist made a mistake.

David's conscience hurt him once the count was done. He admitted he had sinned greatly and acted very foolishly. He asked God to take away his "iniquity," which means the guilt of his sin. A heart that strikes us when we sin is a good sign of God's grace at work. When we confess our sins, we can pray in faith that God will forgive.

God sent the prophet Gad, the "seer" David kept close by for spiritual advice. God's message was to choose one of three punishments. People who are forgiven may still feel the results of their sin in this life. Letting David choose showed God had not cast him off. It also helped David bear the punishment patiently.

The three choices were famine, running from enemies, or plague. Each one would make the people fewer. That fit David's sin, since he had been proud of how many people he had. What we take pride in, God may justly take from us. Older Bibles say "seven years" here, but Chronicles and the Greek translation say three.

David chose to fall into God's hands rather than into the hands of enemies, because God's mercies are great. Enemies would gloat over Israel and do lasting harm. In a plague, David and his family were in as much danger as anyone. In war or famine, a king could protect himself. His choice showed trust in God's goodness even under God's frown.

The plague swept the whole land, and 70,000 people died. Commentators differ on how long it lasted. Some think it ran up to the third day. Others think it stopped that first evening. Joab took nine months to count the people, but the angel passed through the land in a very short time. David's pride in his great numbers was deeply humbled.

As the angel reached out against Jerusalem, God said, "Enough!" "Relented" means God stopped a course of action he had begun. He changed his way, not his mind. God spared the city he had chosen for his temple. The angel stood on Mount Moriah, where God once stopped Abraham from sacrificing Isaac.

David saw the angel and prayed. He took the blame as the shepherd and asked God to punish him and his family instead of the sheep. The people had in fact sinned too, but David was hard on his own sin and gentle about theirs. This reminds readers of Jesus, the Shepherd who was struck so the sheep could be spared.

Gad told David to build an altar on Araunah's threshing floor. A threshing floor was an open-air place for separating grain from straw. God's call to offer sacrifice was a sign he was making peace with David. The spot is thought to be Mount Moriah, where Solomon's temple was later built.
David obeyed God's word through Gad and went up right away. He went in person instead of sending someone. That showed his humility as a sorry king.

Araunah, also called Ornan, was a Jebusite. The Jebusites lived in Jerusalem before Israel took it, and Araunah had likely come to follow Israel's God. He bowed low before the king. David told him he had come to buy the threshing floor and build an altar so the plague would stop. David would not take the land without paying, even as king. God hates robbery dressed up as worship.

Araunah freely offered the land, his oxen, and his wooden farm tools for firewood. He also prayed that God would accept David. He gave like a king, with great generosity. Some think he may once have been a Jebusite ruler. Others read the words simply as "O king." He cared for the king and for the people, and he wanted the plague stopped.

David refused the gift. He would not offer God something that cost him nothing. It was David who had sinned, so the sacrifice had to be his own. A faith that costs nothing is worth little, and our money is given to us to honor God. First Chronicles gives a much larger price. Many explain that the 50 shekels paid for the floor and oxen, and the larger sum bought the whole hill later.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some critical scholars have said the writer of Chronicles purposely made the price larger. Others think one of the numbers was simply copied wrong.

notes.meaning: David built the altar. He offered burnt offerings, which were burned up completely for God, and peace offerings, which gave thanks for God's mercy. God heard the prayers, and the plague stopped. First Chronicles adds that God answered with fire from heaven. Christians see here that peace with God comes through sacrifice, and Christ is our true altar and sacrifice.
